description: HVAC equipment configuration structs and defaults: core config, heating/cooling variants, heat pump, dehumidifier, curves, coil physics, and latent degradation.

reviews.title: HvacCoreConfig defaults vs EnergyPlus Engineering Reference
reviews.prompt: HvacCoreConfig provides defaults for fan_power_per_flow_w_per_m3s, min_plr, crankcase_heater_w. Cross-reference each default against the EnergyPlus Engineering Reference: (a) fan_power_per_flow_w_per_m3s: EnergyPlus default is 773.3 W/(m³/s) for AutoSize (300 CFM/ton with 0.5 in. w.c. external static). If HARES uses a different value, verify the derivation. Typical residential values range 300-600 W/(m³/s) depending on duct static. (b) min_plr (minimum part-load ratio): typical values are 0.2-0.4 for single-stage equipment; below this, the equipment cycles on/off. Verify the default is physically grounded—a min_plr of 0.0 would imply infinite turndown which is impossible for fixed-speed equipment. (c) crankcase_heater_w: typically 30-70W for residential compressor crankcase heaters. Verify the default is in this range and that the heater only operates when the compressor is off and outdoor temperature is below ~10°C (per EnergyPlus logic). (d) Check for any additional EnergyPlus defaults that HARES might have omitted: time constant for part-load cycling, minimum outdoor temperature for compressor operation, maximum outdoor temperature for heat pump heating. Missing defaults produce physically incorrect equipment behavior.

reviews.title: HeatingConfig variants: Furnace, Boiler, Baseboard, HeatPumpHeater defaults
reviews.prompt: All HeatingConfig variants and their defaults. (a) FurnaceConfig: AFUE default (typically 0.78-0.80 for non-condensing, 0.90-0.98 for condensing), capacity (kW), fan power (W). Verify the default AFUE thresholds correctly distinguish condensing from non-condensing furnaces (AFUE > 0.90 implies condensing, which requires condensate drain modeling). (b) BoilerConfig: AFUE default (0.80-0.95), water outlet temperature setpoint, water flow rate, pump power. Verify boiler defaults align with typical residential hydronic systems—outlet temp ~82°C (180°F) for baseboard, lower for radiant. (c) BaseboardConfig: heating capacity per linear meter/foot, thermal time constant. Verify defaults produce reasonable room-by-room heating rates (typically 500-800 W per meter of baseboard). (d) HeatPumpHeaterConfig: HSPF default (HSPF2 of 7.5-10 for modern units), capacity (kW), compressor COP at rated conditions (typically 2.5-4.0 at 8.3°C outdoor). Verify HSPF-to-COP conversion is correct (HSPF is in BTU/Wh, COP is dimensionless; HSPF_region_IV / 3.412 ≈ seasonal average COP). (e) Check that no variant has contradictory defaults (e.g., AFUE > 1.0 which would violate the Second Law).

reviews.title: CoolingConfig variants: AcConfig, RoomAcConfig defaults and airflow
reviews.prompt: All CoolingConfig variants and their defaults. (a) AcConfig (central AC): SEER default (SEER2 of 13.4-15 for modern minimum-efficiency units), SHR (sensible heat ratio) default of 0.75-0.80, CFM/ton default (350-400 CFM/ton; 400 is standard for dry climates, 350 for humid). Verify the CFM/ton to m³/(s·W) conversion: 400 CFM/ton = 400 ft³/min per 12,000 BTU/h ≈ 0.054 m³/(s·kW). (b) RoomAcConfig (window/room AC): typically lower efficiency (CEER or EER instead of SEER), lower SHR (0.65-0.75, meaning more latent capacity as fraction of total), CFM/ton typically 320-350. Verify the distinction between central and room AC defaults is reflected in the code—a room AC with central AC defaults would overestimate efficiency. (c) Compressor type (single-speed, two-speed, variable-speed) must be correctly associated with the part-load degradation model—variable-speed uses different PLF curves than single-speed cycling. (d) EnergyPlus uses different default curves for different compressor types (single-stage DX coil vs variable-speed DX coil); verify HARES matches the EnergyPlus curve selection logic. (e) Check that the cooling default capacity is correctly sized—an undersized default produces unmet cooling hours in the autosizing path.

reviews.title: DehumidifierConfig defaults: water removal, target RH, deadband
reviews.prompt: DehumidifierConfig defaults: rated water removal (30 L/day), target RH (50%), deadband (2.5% RH). Verify physical plausibility: (a) Rated water removal of 30 L/day at 26.7°C and 60% RH: this is a typical residential dehumidifier capacity (50-70 pint/day = 24-33 L/day). Verify the rated condition (DB temperature and RH) matches the EnergyPlus rated condition (26.7°C / 80°F, 60% RH). (b) Target RH of 50%: this is within the typical range of 45-55% for comfort and mold prevention. Verify the target is used correctly—dehumidifier should run when measured RH > target + deadband/2, and stop when RH < target - deadband/2. (c) Deadband of 2.5% RH: a ±1.25% band around 50% target. This is physically reasonable for preventing short-cycling; too narrow (<1%) causes rapid cycling, too wide (>5%) causes large humidity swings. (d) Dehumidifier power at rated condition: typically 300-700W for 30 L/day removal. Verify the energy factor (L/kWh) is in the range 1.5-2.5 L/kWh which is typical for residential units. (e) Part-load performance: dehumidifiers cycle like air conditioners; verify that the part-load fraction (PLF) model is applied correctly, or if the dehumidifier is modeled as constant-efficiency across the operating range.

reviews.title: HeatPumpConfig: dual-mode independence, compressor lockout, defrost
reviews.prompt: HeatPumpConfig supports both heating and cooling in one unit. Verify: (a) Heating and cooling are independently configurable—a heat pump should be able to have different capacities (heating is usually lower than cooling due to lower compressor power at low outdoor temperatures), different efficiencies (HSPF for heating, SEER for cooling), and different airflow rates. Verify the config struct allows these to be specified separately. (b) Compressor lockout temperatures: minimum outdoor temperature for heat pump heating operation (typically -15°C to -25°C for cold-climate heat pumps, -5°C to 0°C for conventional). Below this, the heat pump locks out and supplemental heat (electric resistance or gas furnace) takes over. Also maximum outdoor temperature for heating (typically 15-20°C, above which heating is not needed). Minimum outdoor temperature for cooling (typically 10-15°C, below which economizer can be used). (c) Defrost parameters: defrost initiation temperature threshold (typically -5°C to 5°C outdoor coil temperature), defrost termination temperature/sensor, maximum defrost duration (typically 5-10 minutes), defrost interval (typically 30, 60, or 90 minutes of accumulated compressor runtime), defrost energy consumption (typically auxiliary heat is energized during defrost to prevent cold blow, costing 1-5 kW for 5-10 min). (d) Supplemental heat config: electric resistance strips (5-15 kW typical) or dual-fuel with gas furnace. Verify the supplemental heat control logic—supplemental should not operate simultaneously with the heat pump above the thermal balance point.

reviews.title: Heat pump constants: defrost thresholds, compressor maps, mass flow defaults
reviews.prompt: Heat pump constants module. Verify all constants against EnergyPlus counterparts: (a) Defrost temperature threshold: EnergyPlus uses various defrost strategies; the default time-temperature defrost initiates when outdoor coil temperature < -1°C and defrosts based on accumulated compressor runtime. If HARES uses a fixed temperature, verify it matches the EnergyPlus default. (b) Compressor map defaults: EnergyPlus uses ARI standard rating conditions (heating: 8.33°C outdoor/21.1°C indoor DB; cooling: 35°C outdoor/26.7°C indoor DB). Verify these conditions match the compressor map reference points. The map relates compressor power to outdoor and indoor conditions via biquadratic curves—if the reference conditions differ from the curve's intended reference, all computed powers will be offset. (c) Mass flow rate defaults: refrigerant mass flow rate is typically computed from the compressor map and the enthalpy difference across the condenser/evaporator. Default refrigerant charge and flow rate should be physically plausible for a given capacity—roughly 0.04-0.06 kg/s per kW of cooling capacity for R-410A. (d) Verify the refrigerant properties (density, enthalpy, specific heat) for the default refrigerant (R-410A or R-32) are correct at typical operating conditions. (e) Check for any dimensionless constants that should be 1.0 (e.g., efficiency multipliers at rated conditions) or 0.0 (e.g., degradation at full load) at reference conditions.

reviews.title: Default biquadratic curve coefficient tables: capacity and EIR per speed stage
reviews.prompt: Default biquadratic curve coefficient tables provide capacity and energy input ratio (EIR) as functions of indoor wet-bulb and outdoor dry-bulb temperatures. Verify: (a) The interleaved capacity/EIR coefficient layout is correct for every speed stage. EnergyPlus stores curves as: CAPFT = a + b*T_wb + c*T_wb² + d*T_odb + e*T_odb² + f*T_wb*T_odb, and EIRFT = a + b*T_wb + c*T_wb² + d*T_odb + e*T_odb² + f*T_wb*T_odb. Verify that the coefficients are stored in the correct order (a through f for capacity, then a through f for EIR) and that the correct independent variables (indoor wet-bulb vs dry-bulb) are used. (b) For multi-speed equipment, each speed stage has its own set of coefficients. Verify that the speed index maps correctly to the coefficient position in the table. (c) The curve value at the rated condition (ARI standard 26.7°C indoor WB, 35°C outdoor DB for cooling) must equal 1.0 for both CAPFT and EIRFT—if the coefficients define a curve that does NOT pass through 1.0 at the rated condition, all computed capacities and EIRs are scaled incorrectly. This is a common EnergyPlus error when extracting coefficients from manufacturer data. (d) Verify curve extrapolation bounds: outdoor temperature below -20°C or above 55°C should clamp to the curve value at the min/max, not extrapolate to negative or extreme values. (e) Check normalization: EnergyPlus normalizes capacity and EIR curves to 1.0 at rated conditions; if HARES uses un-normalized curves, the scaling must be applied correctly.

reviews.title: Dehumidifier default curves: EnergyPlus coefficient scaling and conversion
reviews.prompt: Dehumidifier default curves are sourced from EnergyPlus but require unit scaling. Verify: (a) EnergyPlus dehumidifier curves use the form: WaterRemoval = a + b*T_db + c*T_db² + d*RH + e*RH² + f*T_db*RH with different scaling factors. EnergyPlus multiplies d by 100 and e by 10000 (because RH is in percent, 0-100). Verify HARES correctly handles this scaling: if HARES uses RH as fraction [0,1], the scaling must account for the factor-of-100 difference. Incorrect scaling would produce dramatically wrong water removal at high humidity. (b) RATED_DB_C = 26.666 = 80°F exact. This is the EnergyPlus rated condition for dehumidifier performance. Verify this constant is precisely 80°F converted to Celsius (80 - 32) * 5/9 = 26.666...; any rounding (e.g., 26.7) introduces a small error at rated conditions. (c) RH percent-to-fraction conversion: verify all RH inputs/outputs are consistently in percent or fraction throughout the dehumidifier model. A mix of percent in one place and fraction in another is a common integration error. (d) EnergyPlus also applies a quadratic linear minimum curve (WaterRemoval = a + b*T_db) at low RH; verify HARES implements this transition or uses a different approach. (e) Check the coefficient values themselves: for EnergyPlus default residential dehumidifier, a≈0.6, b≈-0.01, c≈0.0002, d≈0.02*100, e≈-0.0002*10000, f≈0.0001*100. Verify HARES values match these within rounding.

reviews.title: Coil physics T_wet fixed-point solver convergence and infinite loop guard
reviews.prompt: The coil physics module uses a fixed-point iteration to solve for coil outlet conditions, particularly the wet-bulb temperature T_wet at the coil surface. Review the convergence behavior for extreme indoor conditions: (a) Very dry conditions (RH < 10%): the coil may operate fully dry, and the wet-bulb fixed-point iteration should converge in 1-2 iterations. Verify the solver detects dry-coil conditions and switches to a simplified model rather than iterating on wet-bulb when latent load is zero. (b) Very humid conditions (RH > 90%): the coil is fully wet and the latent capacity dominates. The fixed-point iteration may require many iterations or may oscillate. Verify convergence criteria include both absolute and relative tolerance on T_wet. (c) Extreme temperature conditions: outdoor 50°C with indoor 30°C at 80% RH—the coil is deeply into wet operation. Ensure the solver does not diverge or produce non-physical temperatures (T_wet > T_db or T_wet < outdoor temperature). (d) No infinite loop: verify there is a maximum iteration count (typically 30-50) with a fallback (use last iteration's value, or an analytical approximation). A common bug is a missing iteration counter that causes an infinite loop when the fixed-point map has slope > 1 near the solution. (e) Under-relaxation: if iteration oscillates, verify that under-relaxation (T_new = α*T_computed + (1-α)*T_old, α ≈ 0.5) is applied or considered. (f) Check the initial guess quality—starting from the previous timestep's converged value provides good convergence; starting from a poor guess (e.g., fixed constant) may need more iterations.

reviews.title: Henderson-Rengarajan latent degradation: parameters and EnergyPlus alignment
reviews.prompt: The Henderson-Rengarajan latent degradation model accounts for reduced moisture removal when the cooling coil cycles on/off (the coil is dry during the off-cycle, so average latent capacity is lower than steady-state). Verify: (a) twet_rated_s = 1500 seconds: this is the time constant for the coil to reach steady-state wetting after startup. EnergyPlus default is 1500s for residential DX coils. If this value is incorrect, the latent degradation during cycling will be wrong—too short overestimates latent removal, too long underestimates it. (b) gamma_rated = 1.5: this is the ratio of initial moisture removal rate to steady-state rate (the coil initially removes more moisture because it's cold and dry at startup). EnergyPlus default is 1.5. Verify this value is consistent with the coil type (DX cooling coil). (c) max_cycling_rate = 3.0 cycles per hour: this limits how many on/off cycles can occur per hour. EnergyPlus default is 3.0 for residential systems. A higher cycling rate would produce more start-up transients and lower average latent performance. Verify that the model respects this limit—if the part-load ratio implies cycling faster than max_cycling_rate, the runtime fraction should be adjusted. (d) latent_time_constant_s = 45 seconds: this is the time constant for the thermal capacity of the coil to respond. Verify this aligns with EnergyPlus's default heat exchanger time constant for DX coils. (e) Verify the latent degradation formula: SHR_actual = SHR_rated * f(PLR, twet_rated, gamma_rated, max_cycling_rate). Check that at PLR=1.0 (continuous operation), SHR_actual = SHR_rated (no degradation), and as PLR decreases, SHR_actual increases (less moisture removal per unit of sensible cooling). The specific EnergyPlus correlation from Henderson and Rengarajan (1996) should be implemented exactly.
